pages.name: Getting Started
pages.content:
Welcome to The Essence System. This page covers everything you need to play a session from inside Foundry.

Your Character Sheet

Open your character's sheet from the Actors sidebar tab. If you don't have a character yet, click Create Character in that same tab, then use the sheet header's wizard button (wand icon) to walk through the full 10-step Character Creation Wizard — it handles Attributes, Skills, Species/Heritage/Distinction, and starting Equipment for you.

Attributes, Skills, and Resources

Your 9 Attributes are grouped into three domains — Physical (Might, Grace, Vigor), Mental (Intellect, Acuity, Resolve), and Spiritual (Presence, Adaptability, Anima). Each domain has a matching Resource (Stamina, Focus, Mana) and Defense (Fortitude, Composure, Harmony), and three Combat Skills. Some skills (Gestalt, Magecraft, Psionics, Ritualism, Calling) are gated — you need the matching Distinction before you can raise them above 0.

Rolling Dice

Click a skill name to roll it. Outside combat you'll pick an Attribute to pair with the skill for an open check. During combat, rolling a skill or an Action/Reaction Card instead spends from your Action Dice or Reaction Dice pool — you choose how many dice to commit (at least the card's minimum, up to whatever's left in the pool), and that many d10s are rolled and deducted from the pool at once.

Wounds

Damage first reduces your Resilience buffer (tracked as Accumulated Damage, reset at the start of each of your Turns). Once it's exceeded, you take a Wound — either a Temporary Wound (if you have any available) or a Core Wound, filled in order: 2 Light, 2 Serious, then 1 Critical. Your Wound State (Unharmed / Lightly / Seriously / Critically Wounded) depends only on how many Core Wound boxes are filled. If you reach Critically Wounded, the Death Track starts advancing at the start of each of your Turns until it's frozen (stabilized) or reaches its end.

Combat

Combat runs through Foundry's own Combat Tracker (the crossed-swords tab in the sidebar). When the GM starts an encounter, click your sheet's Roll Initiative button (or the tracker's own dice icon next to your name — both do the same thing) and choose how many dice to commit: 0 passes, and whatever you don't commit carries over as extra Action Dice on your first Turn. On your Turn, spend Action Dice on cards/skills; at the end of your Turn, click End Turn to convert anything left into Reaction Dice for use on other players' Turns. Burn Dice lets you spend dice straight from a pool without rolling, for costs that call for it (removing a Condition, paying an Echo, etc.).

Combat Style Specialties

Each Combat Skill has its own resource-tracking mechanic (Combo for Prowess, Lock for Ballistics, Threads for Magecraft, and so on) — see the Combat Styles Reference journal for the full rules on each one. Your sheet's Combat tab shows the tracker for any specialty you're currently using.

pages.name: Running a Session
pages.content:
This page covers the GM-side workflow — setting up NPCs, running combat, and managing Conditions.

NPCs and Adversaries

Create an NPC the same way as a Character — from the Actors sidebar tab's Create Actor button, set Type to NPC / Adversary. NPCs use the exact same Attributes/Skills/Resources/Wounds/Combat Dice mechanics as player characters (per the rules: "Game Masters will use those same rules when portraying adversaries"), just without the player-facing fluff (Concept, Career, Non-Combat Skills) — instead they get a Role tag (Minion/Standard/Elite/Nemesis) and a GM Notes field for tactics reminders. Leave NPC tokens unlinked (Foundry's default) so multiple copies of the same monster track wounds independently; Character tokens are force-linked instead, since a PC should always be the one actor.

Portrait Art vs. Token Art

Every Actor (Character or NPC) actually has two separate images: the sheet Portrait (click the art in the sheet header) and the canvas Token Image (what shows when you place it on a scene). Foundry copies the Portrait into the Token Image automatically exactly once — the very first time you set a new Actor's Portrait away from the default placeholder. After that first time, the two are completely independent: changing the Portrait later never touches the Token Image, and vice versa. Click the small pawn-icon button on the corner of the Portrait to set the Token Image directly, without leaving the sheet. Because NPC tokens are unlinked (see above), changing an NPC's Token Image only affects tokens you place after the change — copies already sitting on a scene keep whatever art they were dropped with; drag a fresh token from the sheet to pick up the update, or right-click the placed token → Configure Token to edit it individually.

Running Combat

Combat is driven entirely by Foundry's own Combat Tracker — add combatants, click Begin Combat, and advance rounds/turns from there. Every entry point that rolls Initiative (the tracker's per-combatant dice icon, its Roll All and Roll NPCs buttons, and each sheet's own Roll Initiative button) opens the same dice-commit dialog and produces identical results, so it doesn't matter which one you or your players use. Ending the encounter (deleting the Combat) automatically resets each combatant's combat-state flags and clears any Threads/Authority Specialties that expire at Encounter's end.

Conditions

Conditions live in the Conditions compendium and are also registered as Token HUD status icons — right-click a token, open the status-effects palette, and toggle a Condition on or off directly. This adds or removes a real owned Condition Item on the actor (with whatever mechanical Active Effect the rules define, e.g. Chilled's Movement -2), exactly the same as dragging the Condition Item onto the actor's sheet by hand — use whichever is more convenient in the moment.

Authoring New Content

If you have Foundry's "Create Items" permission (or are a GM), a wand-icon scene-control button opens the Create Content wizard for authoring new Action/Reaction Cards, Equipment, and Conditions straight into the compendium, without hand-building the data model yourself.

Compendiums

Action Cards, Reaction Cards, Conditions, and Equipment ship pre-populated from the live Essence Rules database; Species, Heritages, and Distinctions are hand-authored; and the Combat Styles Reference journal documents every Combat Skill's Specialty mechanic in full. See the system's README for how to refresh this content from the database if the rules change.

pages.name: Role Budget System
pages.content:
Every NPC has a Role tag — Minion, Standard, Elite, or Nemesis — but nothing in the printed rules defines what that tag actually means mechanically. The Monster Creator's Auto-Generate Stat Block needs something to generate from, so this system invents a budget: a plain, tunable table of numbers (kept in module/data/monster-budgets.mjs) that caps what you can hand-enter on a Monster and drives what Auto-Generate rolls up on its own. Treat every number here as homebrew, not canon — revisit it if actual play says a Role feels off.

The Tier Ladder

Four Roles, seven budget axes each. Every axis climbs by the same flat step from one Role to the next — no exponential curves — so you can eyeball roughly how much stronger the next Role up is without doing math. Total Combat Cards (Action + Reaction), for instance, lands on 1 → 3 → 5 → 7: a clean +2 every Role.

RoleAttributesSkillsResilienceTemp WoundsCards (A/R)Equipment
Minion2 pts, max 22 pts, max 21 + 1×Tier01 / 01
Standard7 pts, max 35 pts, max 33 + 2×Tier12 / 12
Elite10 pts, max 48 pts, max 45 + 3×Tier23 / 23
Nemesis13 pts, max 512 pts, max 57 + 4×Tier34 / 34

Resilience Scales With Tier

Resilience is the one axis that is a formula rather than a flat number, since a Tier 5 Minion shouldn't take the same hit before Wounds start as a Tier 1 one. Resilience = Base + Per-Tier × Tier, both of which climb with Role:

RoleTier 1Tier 3Tier 5
Minion246
Standard5913
Elite81420
Nemesis111927

How Auto-Generate Spends the Budget

The one-button path on the Concept step rolls the whole stat block in this order, then hands every result back to you to hand-edit exactly like the rest of the Monster Creator. Each step below also has its own Reroll button for redoing just that part.

  1. Attributes & Skills — a weighted point-buy: each point is a coin-flip weighted 3-to-1 toward whichever Domain you picked as the Emphasis (Physical/Mental/Spiritual), enough to lean the roll without ever locking the other two Domains out. Skills respect the same five Distinction gates a player would: Gestalt (requires Gifted), Magecraft (Arcanist), Psionics (Psyker), Ritualism (Invoker), and Calling (Summoner) only receive points if the matching Distinction is already attached.
  2. Resilience, Temporary Wounds, Equipment Limit — set directly from the Role/Tier budget table above, no randomness.
  3. Combat Cards — every owned Action/Reaction Card is cleared and re-picked from the qualifying pool, weighted 3-to-1 toward the three Skills the Attribute/Skill roll happened to land highest on, so a Nemesis that rolled heavy Ritualism tends to walk away with Ritualism cards.
  4. Equipment — a straight random draw from the Equipment compendium, capped at the Role's Equipment count.

Tuning It

Every number above is a plain object literal in module/data/monster-budgets.mjs — nothing else in the system reasons about the exact values, so any of them can be edited directly. A retuned number takes effect on the very next sheet opened; no migration, no data to rebuild.

pages.name: How It Works
pages.content:
Full Manifestation is Calling's most dramatic option: instead of a summoned creature acting alongside you, your character is replaced by one of 8 spirit bodies for the rest of the Encounter. This page covers the shared procedure every profile follows; the mechanical details (numbers, penalties, exact wording) are drafted in the project's PLAYTEST_RULES.md and CALLING_PROFILES.md source documents, and the 8 profiles themselves live in the Calling Full Manifestations compendium as NPC Actors — see "Running It as a GM" for how those get assigned to a character.

Entering

Resolve an eligible Calling card as normal, paying its own cost. After it resolves, you may pay an additional toll to transform: burn 3 more Action Dice plus Mana equal to the card's Rank + 1 (the Summoner Origin reduces the die burn to 2). Rolled dice can't also pay this burn, and a Reaction can never manifest a form. Which of the 8 bodies you can choose is gated by Calling Rank: Rank 0 offers Familiar or Sprite, Rank 1 adds Beast/Phantom/Golem, Rank 2 adds Elemental/Ancestor/Fey.

What Carries Over

You are not gaining a second creature or a fresh turn. The form replaces you in your current space and uses your turn exactly as it stood: whatever Action Dice and Reaction Dice you have left remain exactly that many, your Movement already spent this turn stays spent, and your own ongoing Wounds and Conditions are still true underneath the new body — transforming heals nothing. Your Accumulated Damage pressure (see "Damage & Wounds Across Forms") also carries over rather than resetting.

What You Can Do While Manifested

Only that profile's own 2-3 built-in maneuvers (Actions/Reactions, tagged Manifestation in the compendium so they're never confused with the 396-card catalogue) plus compatible universal Basics — not any learned card from any Style. Maneuvers use your own Calling Rank and Attribute ratings to determine dice, never a stat on the profile Actor itself; no Expertise is required and no Mastery Surge is granted. Your normal weapon and armor sit out of play and add nothing to a profile's intrinsic maneuvers.

Leaving

Burn 1 Action Die on your turn to voluntarily dismiss, returning to your own space (or the nearest legal empty one). You can't switch directly from one form into another — dismiss first, then use a later Calling card to enter something else. The first subtype you fully manifest into during an Encounter is locked in for that whole Encounter: you can dismiss and re-enter that same body as many times as you like, but you cannot rotate through different bodies in one fight.

pages.name: Damage & Wounds Across Forms
pages.content:
Each profile has its own small Wound track (3-5 boxes, same Light/Light/Serious/Serious/Critical severity pattern as a character's usual 5-box track, just truncated). This track is separate from your own Core Wounds and, per the rules, persists for the entire Adventure — not just one fight. In this system that persistence is literal: the profile is a real NPC Actor, and its Wound boxes simply stay marked between sessions until Downtime treats them.

The Shared Pressure Counter

Accumulated Damage (the pressure that has to exceed Resilience before a hit becomes a real Wound) belongs to you, not to whichever body is currently active, and it does not reset just because you transformed, dismissed, or were defeated. When the next hit for amount x lands against whichever Resilience R is currently active:

new Wounds = max(0, D + x - R) - max(0, D - R)

...then D becomes D + x. This prevents switching bodies from erasing pressure you'd already built up, and prevents being charged twice for a hit you already absorbed.

Worked example: D is 2 when you enter a Golem (Resilience 2). Entry itself adds no Wound. A following hit for 1 Damage causes max(0, 3-2) - max(0, 2-2) = 1 Wound to the Golem; D becomes 3. Dismissing afterward does not reset D or undo that Wound.

Defeat

When a hit fills a profile's last Wound box, the form collapses immediately: any Wounds from that same hit beyond the track's remaining capacity transfer to you, and you additionally suffer 1 feedback Wound just from being forced out (Temporary Wounds can absorb either). You return to your own body, and that specific subtype is marked Broken until Downtime — your other subtypes remain available. No profile ability heals, restores Resources, removes a Wound, or suppresses a Critical Wound's incapacitating effect.

A profile marked Living is a valid target for a living-only effect; one marked Nonliving is not, but otherwise still feels pain, can be restrained, and is affected by mental attacks, magic, forced movement and ordinary Conditions like anything else — being a Phantom does not confer incorporeality.

These numbers are provisional playtest values, not finalized adversary statistics — compare them against your table's actual characters before treating them as settled.

pages.name: Running It as a GM
pages.content:
The 8 profiles live pre-built in the Calling Full Manifestations compendium as NPC Actors, each already carrying its 2-3 maneuvers as owned Action/Reaction Cards — open one from the compendium to read its full stat block and maneuver text exactly like any other NPC.

Assigning a Profile to a Character

A compendium document can't hold Wounds or player ownership, so the first time a character fully manifests a given subtype, drag that profile from the compendium into the world (or duplicate it) to create that character's own persistent copy — this is what makes the Wound record actually persist across sessions, since it's just a normal world Actor that never gets deleted. Grant the controlling player Owner permission on it so they can open and act from it directly, the same as opening their own character's sheet. If that same character manifests the same subtype again later, reuse this same world copy rather than creating another one.

Swapping Control

While manifested, the simplest way to run it at the table is to swap which Actor the character's combat token represents — point the token at the profile Actor for the duration, then back at the character's own Actor on dismissal or defeat. The Combat Tracker's turn order doesn't need to change; only which sheet the player is looking at does.

Not Yet Automated

This guide documents the ruling, not a one-click tool — entering/dismissing/defeat and the Accumulated Damage carryover above are currently tracked by hand, the same way Contingency, Threads, and the other Combat Style Specialties are. Treat every number and interaction here as a provisional playtest draft, not finalized canon.
